t.4.54.1: Having heard Hanumān's words, courteous, consistent with dharma, and full of respect for his master, Aṅgada spoke these words.
t.4.54.2: Steadfastness, purity in every respect, freedom from cruelty and uprightness, together with deeds of valour and fortitude, are not found in Sugrīva.
t.4.54.3: He who, while still living, takes as his own the wife of his elder brother, the beloved chief queen who by dharma is his mother, is despicable.
t.4.54.4: How can he know dharma, that evil-minded brother by whom, though he had been appointed to stand by during the battle, the mouth of the cave was sealed?
t.4.54.5: He by whom Rāghava has been forgotten, Rāghava of great fame, whose hand was clasped in a pledge of truth and who has already done his deed, whose good deed would such a one ever remember?
t.4.54.6: He by whom we were commanded to search for Sītā out of fear of Lakṣmaṇa, and not because he was timid with fear of adharma, how could there be dharma in such a one?
t.4.54.7: What noble man of his own lineage who wishes to live would ever place his trust in that sinful, ungrateful one, who forgets what is owed and whose mind is fickle?
t.4.54.8: Whether he is virtuous or devoid of virtue, once Sugrīva has established his own son in the kingship, how will he let me live, born as I am of his enemy's lineage?
t.4.54.9: With my counsel betrayed, guilty of an offense and bereft of power, how indeed could I reach Kiṣkindhā and go on living there, feeble, like one who has no protector?
t.4.54.10: For Sugrīva, deceitful, cruel and pitiless, would subject me to secret punishment or to imprisonment for the sake of the kingdom.
t.4.54.11: Better for me than imprisonment and ruin is to fast unto death. Give me leave, all of you, and let the vānaras go back to their homes.
t.4.54.12: I promise you, I will not go to the city; right here I will sit in a fast unto death, for death alone is better for me.
t.4.54.13: Then the king, my younger kinsman Sugrīva, lord of the monkeys, should be addressed first with a respectful salutation and also with an inquiry after his welfare.
t.4.54.14: My mother Rumā should be told of my welfare, with wishes for her good health first, and you ought also to console my mother Tārā.
t.4.54.16: Having spoken these words and saluted the elders as well, Aṅgada, dejected and weeping, lay down upon the ground on darbha grass.
t.4.54.15: By nature fond of her son, compassionate and pitiable, she, on hearing that I have perished here, will surely give up her life.
t.4.54.19: Understanding that resolve of Vālin's son, the bulls among the monkeys all touched water and sat down facing east on darbha grass with its tips pointing south, having taken their place on the northern shore.
t.4.54.17: As he lay down there, the bulls among the monkeys, weeping and stricken with grief, shed hot tears from their eyes.
t.4.54.18: Censuring Sugrīva and praising Vālin, they all gathered around Aṅgada and resolved to sit in a fast unto death.
t.4.54.20: As the many monkeys, each as large as the peak of a great mountain, settled upon it, that mountain had the hollows of its cascades made to resound by them, as if by mighty clouds thundering loudly.
